blocks.title: Catalyst
blocks.text: A catalyst is defined as a substance which alters the rate of a chemical reaction, but remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.

A catalyst is often present in a very small amount. For example, the reaction between H₂ and O₂ to form water is very slow at ordinary temperature, but proceeds more rapidly in the presence of platinum. Platinum acts as a catalyst. Similarly, KClO₃ decomposes much more rapidly in the presence of a small amount of MnO₂. HCl is oxidized to Cl₂ in the presence of CuCl₂.

The process, which takes place in the presence of a catalyst, is called catalysis. A catalyst provides a new reaction path with a low activation energy barrier, as shown in Figure 7.8. A greater number of molecules are now able to get over the new energy barrier and reaction rate increases.

blocks.alt: Energy against progress of reaction. A Reactants level on the left and a lower Products level on the right. A tall blue hump (uncatalysed) and a lower red hump (catalysed) join the two levels. Double-headed arrows from the reactant level show 'Activation Energy without catalyst' (blue, to the top of the blue hump) and 'Activation Energy with catalyst' (red, to the top of the red hump).
blocks.caption: Figure 7.8: The energy path diagram for an uncatalyzed and a catalyzed reaction (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed label 'Activaton Energy without catalyst' misspells activation.
In this process, the catalyst and the reactants are in the same phase and the reacting system is homogeneous throughout. The catalyst is distributed uniformly throughout the system.
i. The formation of SO₃(g) from SO₂(g) and O₂(g) in the contact process for the manufacture of sulphuric acid, needs NO(g) as a catalyst. Both the reactants and the catalyst are gases.
book_errors: in the contact process for the manufacture of sulphuric acid

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: NO(g) is the catalyst of the old lead-chamber process, not the contact process. In the lead-chamber process the oxidation of SO₂(g) by O₂(g) to SO₃(g) is catalysed by NO(g); all are gases, so this is homogeneous catalysis. The contact process uses solid V₂O₅, which is heterogeneous catalysis.
ii. Esters are hydrolyzed in the presence of H₂SO₄. Both the reactants and the catalyst are in the solution state.

blocks.text_alt: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(l) (ethyl ethanoate) + H₂O(l) →(H⁺) CH₃COOH(l) (ethanoic acid) + CH₃CH₂OH(l) (ethanol)

blocks.title: Did you Know!
blocks.text: Biochemical catalysts, commonly known as enzymes (nature’s catalyst) are essential molecules in living organisms’ function by lowering the activation energy required for a chemical reaction to proceed, thereby increasing the reaction rate. Enzymes are typically proteins. Factors such as pH, temperature, and the concentration of substrate molecules can influence enzyme activity.
In such systems, the catalyst and the reactants are in different phases. Mostly, the catalysts are in the solid phase, while the reactants are in the gaseous or liquid phase. For example:
Oxidation of ammonia to NO in the presence of platinum gauze helps us to manufacture HNO₃.
Hydrogenation of unsaturated organic compounds are catalysed by finely divided Ni, Pd or Pt.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Vitamins are organic compounds that act as catalysts in biochemical reactions, especially when they function as coenzymes. Coenzymes are organic molecules that help enzymes catalyze reactions more efficiently. For example, Vitamin K, is necessary for blood clotting. Low levels of vitamin K can cause bleeding diathesis. A lack of vitamins can disrupt metabolic balance in cells and organisms. Vitamin deficiency is an example of a cofactor deficiency.

blocks.prompt: a) Can a catalyst be consumed in a chemical reaction? Why or why not?
blocks.explanation: No. By definition a catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction. It may take part in intermediate steps, but it is regenerated at the end.

blocks.prompt:
b) Explain whether the reaction below is an example of heterogeneous or homogeneous catalysis:
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)
blocks.explanation: Homogeneous: with NO(g) as the catalyst (as in the text), the reactants (SO₂, O₂) and the catalyst are all in the gas phase.

blocks.prompt:
c) Draw an energy profile diagram to show a typical uncatalysed reaction and an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
On your diagram show:
i) the activation energy for the catalysed and
ii) uncatalysed reactions
blocks.explanation: Both curves start at the same reactants level and end at the same products level. The uncatalysed hump is high (larger activation energy); the enzyme hump is much lower (smaller activation energy). Show each activation energy by an arrow from the reactants level to the peak of its hump.

answer_figure.alt: Energy profile, energy against progress of reaction. The reactants and products lines are the same for both curves. The blue curve (without catalyst) has a high peak, the red curve (with enzyme) a low peak. Arrows from the reactants level to each peak: blue 'Ea without catalyst' is long, red 'Ea with enzyme' is short.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: energy profile of an uncatalysed and an enzyme-catalysed reaction, with both activation energies
answer_figure.long_description: Both routes start from the same reactants and end at the same products, so ΔH does not change. The enzyme provides a new route with a much lower energy barrier. The blue arrow is the activation energy without a catalyst and the red arrow the one with the enzyme; the red arrow is shorter, so more molecules cross the barrier and the reaction is faster.
